title: Mannheim water allocation policy adopted
subtitle: Side stream treatment pilot update, development rules, conservation plans, and an invited outside expert presentation.
overview: Regional Council held a special meeting on the Mannheim Service Area water capacity constraint. After a closed session on potential litigation, Council heard from four delegations and received two staff reports on work underway and the approach to development. Council adopted a Water Supply Capacity Allocation Policy for the Mannheim Service Area {{vote:m4}}. Under it, the Region will share new capacity with area municipalities in proportion to forecast population and employment growth, and each municipality will decide which projects receive water.

The policy sets the framework only. Actual allocation amounts depend on an Interim Risk Management Framework that staff plan to bring to Council on June 3. Staff said the figures shown at the meeting were illustrative. For residents and builders, new water capacity will be handed out in stages, at first quarterly, and each municipality will need its own policy.

Council also voted to invite a groundwater expert to present for 20 minutes on May 20 or May 28 {{vote:m3}}. Staff reported that the side stream treatment pilot is tentatively due to start in the third quarter of 2026. The Regional Chair said she had invited the provincial land and development facilitator to help, and that options including more supply from the Wilmot Waterfield would be considered. An outdoor water restriction by-law takes effect May 31.

decisions.detail: Council adopted the Water Supply Capacity Allocation Policy for the Mannheim Service Area and directed staff to implement it, with the added words "in conjunction with area municipalities" for region-wide benefit projects {{vote:m4}}.
Council directed staff to invite a groundwater expert to give a 20-minute presentation at a Council meeting on either May 20 or May 28, 2026 {{vote:m3}}.

debate: Delegates from the development industry said a freeze on new development is in effect, and that lenders and funders are losing confidence and some projects are under financial strain. They asked for allocation numbers by early June and for access to the Region's water data, including a month-by-month supply and demand model.

A homebuilders' representative asked that the policy have a clear end point, apply consistently across area municipalities, recognise projects already in the pipeline, and use a transparent allocation method developed with industry. Several delegates said working group meetings leave too little room for real discussion. Staff replied that later meetings were given double the time and workshop formats.

A planning consultant asked that private fire hydrant requirements be left out of capacity calculations. Staff said fire protection sizing does not add demand and will not be counted in new demand calculations.

A developer asked staff to treat a demolished factory site as a reduction in demand. Staff said demolished buildings generally drop out of flow calculations after 12 months. One councillor suggested checking that allocations reflect actual data.

Councillors disagreed on hearing the outside expert. Supporters wanted transparency, the chance to ask questions and trust-building. Opponents said it could reintroduce disputed information and set back progress toward the June 3 decision. One councillor said they might not support the allocation policy until their own municipality's staff confirmed the percentages.
